title: Logical Conclusions in R&D - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: See how drawing Logical Conclusions from your experimental results completes the systematic R&D cycle in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: Logical conclusions are the step in Canada's SR&ED "How" requirement where claimants draw conclusions from experiment or analysis findings after testing a hypothesis. For taxpayers claiming federal SR&ED incentives under the Income Tax Act, contemporaneous records must show a logical progression from experimental premise to result; vague records can defeat a claim.

body.text: Logical conclusions are the step in Canada's SR&ED "How" requirement where claimants draw conclusions from experiment or analysis findings after testing a hypothesis. For taxpayers claiming federal SR&ED incentives under the Income Tax Act, contemporaneous records must show a logical progression from experimental premise to result; vague records can defeat a claim.

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive regime—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under sections 37, 127, 127.1, and 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (ITA)—has undergone its most sweeping statutory modernization in more than a decade between late 2024 and November 2026. With Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) on March 26, 2026, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, broadened the prior-year taxable-capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15 million–$75 million three-year average revenue phase-out, and restored eligibility for both SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched a voluntary Pre-Claim Approval process providing up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks for eligible Canadian businesses earning under $25,000,000 in annual gross income.

Two major fiscal developments further reshape corporate R&D tax planning across Canada as of November 2026. Provincially, Québec's Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), administered by Revenu Québec, replaced eight legacy Québec R&D tax credits and researcher tax holidays for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, introducing a consolidated 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold (and 20% above $1,000,000), inclusive of new capital equipment. Federally, Budget 2026—tabled on November 5, 2026—proposes to expand SR&ED eligibility for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, to include initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs. Because Budget 2026 measures (alongside the previously announced September 15, 2026 Productivity Mega Deduction) remain legislative proposals accompanied by Notices of Ways and Means Motions pending Royal Assent, claimants must strictly separate enacted Bill C-15 provisions from unlegislated Budget 2026 proposals when preparing current tax returns.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution (2024–2026)
1.1 Core Federal Statutory Framework under the Income Tax Act and Regulations

Canada's federal SR&ED program is a statutory tax entitlement codified in the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX (section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Unlike discretionary innovation grants capped by annual departmental envelopes, SR&ED incentives operate through the self-assessment income tax system: any resident taxpayer or Canadian branch of a non-resident enterprise carrying on business in Canada that conducts eligible SR&ED work in Canada, incurs allowable expenditures, and satisfies mandatory statutory filing deadlines is legally entitled to claim SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits.

Four foundational provisions of the Income Tax Act, supported by section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, govern every federal SR&ED claim. First, subsection 248(1) defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research (paragraph (a)), applied research (paragraph (b)), experimental development (paragraph (c)), and eight enumerated disciplines of directly supporting work (paragraph (d)), while excluding commercial, routine, or non-scientific activities under paragraphs (e) through (k). Second, section 37 establishes a cumulative, discretionary pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (subsection 37(1)), incorporating current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and restored post-December 15, 2024 capital and lease outlays (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B)), reduced by government and non-government assistance (paragraph 37(1)(d)) and prior-year ITCs claimed or refunded (paragraph 37(1)(e)), and enforced by a strict 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting bar (subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1)).

Third, section 127 governs Investment Tax Credit calculation and application against Part I federal tax otherwise payable (subsection 127(5)), partnership ITC allocations (subsection 127(8)), core statutory definitions of "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," and "eligible Canadian public corporation" (subsection 127(9)), the 20% enhanced ITC rate addition (subsection 127(10.1)), expenditure limit formulas and group allocations (subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.63)), non-arm's-length cost adjustments (subsection 127(11.6)), assistance and contract reductions (subsections 127(18) to 127(20)), and ITC recapture (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)). Fourth, section 127.1 establishes cash refundability for unused ITCs (subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)), defines "qualifying corporation" status and the qualifying income limit (subsection 127.1(2)), and deems any refunded ITC to have been deducted against Part I tax (subsection 127.1(3)). Within the Income Tax Regulations, paragraph 2900(2)(c) defines directly attributable overhead under the traditional method, subsection 2900(4) sets the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), and subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) govern specified-employee proxy salary-base caps and exclusions.
1.2 Enacted Bill C-15 Reforms (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and Transitional Cut-Off Rules

The current federal framework reflects a two-stage legislative expansion enacted in early 2026. The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) initially proposed raising the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, widening the taxable-capital phase-out thresholds, extending the enhanced 35% rate to ECPCs, and restoring SR&ED capital expenditures. Federal Budget 2025 (Canada Strong Budget 2025) confirmed those structural reforms and further raised the enhanced expenditure limit to $6,000,000. Parliament enacted the full Budget 2025 SR&ED package in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, 45th Parliament, 1st Session), which received Royal Assent on Thursday, March 26, 2026.

Because Bill C-15 applies retroactively to December 2024, auditors and corporate claimants must distinguish between two statutory effective-date triggers. First, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out corridor, and ECPC access to the 35% enhanced ITC apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024. Eligibility depends exclusively on the start date of the taxation year rather than its year-end. Thus, a calendar-year corporation whose fiscal year began January 1, 2025 qualifies for the $6,000,000 limit across both its 2025 and 2026 returns, whereas a corporation whose fiscal year ran from December 1, 2024 to November 30, 2025 remains governed by the legacy $3,000,000 limit and $10 million–$50 million phase-out for that entire 2025 year. If a corporation with a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024 already filed under the legacy $3,000,000 cap prior to March 26, 2026, it may amend its claim provided its 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline has not yet elapsed.

Second, restored eligibility for SR&ED capital expenditures (including Shared-Use Equipment) and equipment lease costs operates on a transaction-date trigger, applying strictly to depreciable property acquired (and available for use) and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024, and lease outlays incurred before December 16, 2024, do not qualify for SR&ED deductions or ITCs under any circumstances. Where a claimant's taxation year straddled December 15, 2024 (having begun before December 16, 2024), SR&ED operating-time percentages for leased equipment must be calculated solely as a percentage of total operating time occurring after December 15, 2024.
1.3 Federal Budget 2026 Proposals (November 5, 2026) and Complementary Tax Measures

On November 5, 2026, the federal government tabled Budget 2026, proposing two downstream expansions to the SR&ED program to support late-stage commercialization and domestic intellectual property retention, carrying a projected five-year federal fiscal cost of $930 million ($25 million in 2026–27, $200 million in 2027–28, $245 million in 2028–29, $225 million in 2029–30, and $235 million in 2030–31).

Under the first Budget 2026 measure, eligible SR&ED activities would expand to include regulatory and certification testing—specifically tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification needed to commercialize a product or process. To qualify, these validation activities must directly relate to a project eligible under the SR&ED program's existing rules, and they attract the same eligible expenditure categories as core SR&ED (salaries and wages, materials, contracting costs, overhead, and machinery and equipment).

Under the second Budget 2026 measure, eligible SR&ED expenditures would expand to include costs reasonably incurred to obtain (prepare and file applications) and periodically maintain intellectual property (IP) protection for IP developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project. Qualifying IP rights are restricted to four statutory categories—patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software—protected under Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation. Administrative fees paid to foreign IP offices qualify, whereas supporting preparation activities qualify only if conducted in Canada. Costs incurred to enforce IP rights (such as infringement litigation) and outlays not directly connected to securing or maintaining IP rights are explicitly excluded. Furthermore, if a taxpayer disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was claimed on IP protection costs, recapture rules will claw back the related SR&ED deductions and ITCs.

Per the Budget 2026 Tax Measures: Supplementary Information, the proposed SR&ED expansions apply to taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day (November 5, 2026), with legal practitioners also noting transitional provisions tied to Royal Assent of implementing legislation. Because Budget 2026 proposals are accompanied by Notices of Ways and Means Motions and had not received Royal Assent as of mid-November 2026, businesses should track qualifying regulatory validation and IP filing projects prospectively without altering filed claim calculations until Parliament enacts an implementing bill.

Budget 2026 also confirmed the government's intention to proceed with the Productivity Mega Deduction—first announced on September 15, 2026—an accelerated capital-cost and Canadian development expense measure estimated to cost $36 billion over five years beginning in 2026–27. While Class 1 buildings are excluded from the Productivity Mega Deduction, qualifying manufacturing and processing buildings remain eligible for the separate temporary immediate-expensing measure announced in Budget 2025. In addition, Budget 2026 opened a formal consultation (with submissions due January 8, 2027) on a potential corporate-group current-year non-capital loss transfer mechanism. Both the Productivity Mega Deduction and group loss transfers remain unlegislated as of November 2026.

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Outs, and Carryovers
2.1 Dual-Pronged Incentive Mechanics: Section 37 Pool and Section 127 Investment Tax Credits

Federal SR&ED relief delivers two distinct, sequential mechanisms. Under the first prong (subsection 37(1)), allowable current SR&ED expenditures—employee salaries and wages, consumed or transformed materials, 100% of SR&ED contract and third-party payments, post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs, and traditional-method overhead—together with 100% of restored post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital expenditures enter a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. A claimant may deduct any portion up to 100% of this pool in computing current-year business income for tax purposes, or carry unused pool balances forward indefinitely to shelter taxable income in future years. If the claimant elects the proxy method to calculate overhead, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is never added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool because actual overhead outlays are already deducted as ordinary business expenses.

Under the second prong (sections 127 and 127.1), Canada administers a purely volume-based Investment Tax Credit with no base-period incremental spending hurdle and no upper ceiling on total claimable SR&ED expenditures. Taxpayers earn either the 15% basic ITC (subsection 127(9)) or, for eligible CCPCs and ECPCs within their annual expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC—computed as the 15% basic rate plus a 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1). Qualified expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit continue to earn the 15% basic ITC without cap. Because SR&ED tax credits are themselves taxable relief under Canadian law, any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a taxation year reduces the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e) and, to the extent it exceeds the pool balance, is included in the following year's taxable income.
2.2 Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Mechanics for CCPCs and ECPCs

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC is $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in enhanced ITCs), shared across an associated CCPC group or a consolidated ECPC group. Two parallel statutory formulas govern the gradual phase-out of this $6,000,000 limit:

Under Subsection 127(10.2) (CCPC Taxable-Capital Method), unless a CCPC elects to use the revenue method, its $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (aggregated across all associated CCPCs) in the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000. Specifically, the expenditure limit equals $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil when prior-year combined taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise equals the excess over $15,000,000 up to a maximum of $60,000,000. Every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by exactly $100,000. Corporate tax planners must track a critical post-Bill C-15 divergence: the federal $500,000 Small Business Deduction (SBD) business limit (section 125) still grinds down over the legacy $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 prior-year taxable-capital range (and grinds down for passive investment income above $50,000). Consequently, a CCPC with $55,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital loses 100% of its SBD while still retaining a $2,000,000 SR&ED expenditure limit.

Under Subsection 127(10.6) (ECPC and Electing CCPC Three-Year Average Revenue Method), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—defined in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act as corporations resident in Canada that are public corporations, are not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, and satisfy an additional control test based on publicly available information, or eligible subsidiaries of such corporations—compute their $6,000,000 expenditure limit reduction using average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years rather than taxable capital. Crucially, a CCPC can also opt out of the taxable-capital grind and elect into this three-year average revenue formula by filing a prescribed election under subsection 127(10.31) (standalone CCPC) or subsection 127(10.32) (CCPC with associated corporations)—preventing large equity financings from eroding the 35% credit for pre-revenue or early-revenue technology and life-sciences firms. Under subsection 127(10.6), the expenditure limit decreases once three-year average annual financial-statement revenue exceeds $15,000,000 and becomes nil at $75,000,000, following the same $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000] slope. For an ECPC belonging to a consolidated group (subsection 127(10.61)), the $6,000,000 limit is shared across the group and annual revenue is drawn from the group's consolidated financial statements as a single economic entity (including entities joining or leaving during the year). Where associated group members prepare separate financial statements, revenue across all current group members for the preceding three fiscal years is totalled—regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year period—with reasonable adjustments permitted to eliminate intra-group sales.

Associated CCPCs allocate their shared expenditure limit annually on T2 Schedule 49 (subsection 127(10.3)), subject to Ministerial allocation if a group fails to file an agreement (subsections 127(10.4) for CCPCs and 127(10.63) for ECPCs). Short taxation years (shorter than 51 weeks) or multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year alongside an associated CCPC require strict day-count proration (Days in Tax Year ÷ 365) under subsection 127(10.5). Anti-avoidance rules also deem two or more corporations to be associated where one of the main reasons for their separate existence is to reduce income tax payable or multiply refundable SR&ED ITCs.
2.3 Qualifying Corporation Status, Refundability Tiers, and Carryover Rules

Cash refundability of unused SR&ED ITCs under section 127.1 depends on entity classification, whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" or an "excluded corporation", whether spending falls within or above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, and whether outlays are current expenditures / PPA versus capital expenditures. Under subsection 127.1(2), a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" if its prior-year taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 updated the Qualifying Income Limit formula to $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is prior-year combined taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000 (capped at $60,000,000), reaching nil at $75,000,000. Qualifying-corporation status no longer affects the 35% enhanced ITC within the $6,000,000 limit (which is 100% refundable on current/PPA costs and 40% refundable on capital costs for both qualifying and non-qualifying CCPCs other than excluded corporations, as well as for ECPCs); rather, qualifying-corporation status determines solely whether a CCPC receives 40% refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above its expenditure limit.

3. Technical Eligibility Criteria and Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures
3.1 Statutory Definition of Eligible SR&ED Work, Support Work, and Exclusions

To qualify for SR&ED tax incentives under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, work must be conducted in Canada in a field of natural science or engineering (conforming generally to the OECD Frascati Manual) and satisfy both the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement articulated in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. Under the "Why" requirement, the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement—attempting to generate or discover new scientific or technological knowledge to resolve a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty. Diagnostic signs that existing technological knowledge is insufficient include inapplicable existing design methods, specifications outside normal operating ranges or standards, excessive unknown variables, evolving problem dynamics, unavailable baseline data, or interlocking engineering constraints. Acquiring existing industry know-how—through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert consultants, or buying proprietary licences—never constitutes technological advancement. Conversely, an experiment that fails to meet commercial targets still qualifies if it resolves technological uncertainty and advances knowledge. Under the "How" requirement, the claimant must execute a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis: defining the technological obstacle, formulating a testable hypothesis consistent with known facts, planning and testing that hypothesis through experiment or analysis, drawing logical conclusions from the findings, and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

Core eligible SR&ED (paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c)) comprises basic research (advancing scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as characterizing a newly discovered virus), applied research (advancing scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as investigating viral mechanisms to develop a vaccine), and experimental development (achieving technological advancement to create new, or incrementally improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, such as resolving scale-up process uncertainties for rapid vaccine manufacturing). In addition, paragraph 248(1)(d) allows support work that is commensurate with the needs (in amount, size, extent, and duration) and directly supports core SR&ED, strictly limited to eight statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research.
By contrast, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) statutorily exclude seven categories of work that can never be claimed:

items: Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (paragraph (f));
Research in the social sciences or the humanities (paragraph (g));
Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (paragraph (h));
Commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (i));

body.text: Where an activity such as testing or data collection overlaps in appearance with an exclusion, purpose governs: tasks carried out specifically and exclusively to support experimental investigation qualify under paragraph (d), whereas multipurpose or commercial-readiness activities are excluded. Claimants may group eligible activities from multiple business projects into a single Form T661 SR&ED project whenever those activities pursue the same technological advancement.
3.2 Salaries, Wages, 180-Day Payment Rule, Foreign Work, and Specified Employee Caps

Employee salaries and wages represent the highest-leverage SR&ED cost category, particularly under the proxy method where $100,000 of eligible direct salary yields $155,000 of qualified expenditures ($100,000 wages plus $55,000 PPA), compared with $100,000 for materials and $80,000 for arm's-length Canadian contractors. Claimable wages are restricted to employees directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED, eligible paragraph (d) support work, or direct technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects (assigning technological staff, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, or specifying experimental material quality)—determined strictly by actual tasks performed rather than job titles. Under the CRA SR&ED payment rule, salaries and wages must be incurred and paid in the taxation year or paid within 180 days of the tax year-end to qualify. While SR&ED must generally take place in Canada (excluding foreign branches of resident companies), narrow statutory provisions referenced in subsection 37(2) and the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy govern permissible SR&ED wages outside Canada: under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), salary or wages paid to employees resident in Canada for SR&ED carried on outside Canada solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada are deemed incurred in Canada, up to 10% of the claimant's total salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Strict statutory ceilings tied to the Canada Pension Plan Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE)—officially set at $71,300 for 2025 and $74,600 for 2026—apply to specified employees (whose ownership/arm's-length definition and direct-wage bonus rules are detailed in section 6.0 of the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy). First, claimable direct SR&ED salary or wages for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends ($356,500 for 2025 and $373,000 for 2026). Second, under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, the amount included in the proxy salary base for a specified employee is capped at the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year), or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE prorated for the number of days of employment in the taxation year via 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed ÷ 365) ($178,250 for a full 365-day year ending in 2025 and $186,500 in 2026, with no proration for part-year non-specified status, and subject to group-allocation rules where employed by associated corporations).
3.3 Overhead Methods, Cloud/Software Costs, Materials, Subcontractors, and Third-Party Payments

Claimants choose annually on Form T661 between two overhead calculation methods. The Proxy Method (subsection 2900(4) ITR) adds a flat 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on the eligible direct SR&ED salary base to qualified expenditures without tracking individual overhead invoices. Conversely, the Traditional Method (paragraph 2900(2)(c) ITR) claims actual overhead and other current expenditures directly attributable and incremental to prosecuting SR&ED in Canada on Line 360 of Form T661. Under the CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, software licences and cloud computing outlays are treated as overhead expenditures. Consequently, claimants using the Proxy Method cannot claim software or cloud computing fees separately—doing so is disallowed by the CRA as an "overhead on overhead" expenditure—whereas claimants using the Traditional Method may claim incremental, directly attributable cloud and software outlays.

Under the CRA SR&ED Materials Policy, materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed, including upstream processing such as third-party galvanization of metal parts prior to destructive SR&ED testing) and materials transformed (integrated into prototypes or trial runs retaining commercial value) qualify at 100% of cost whether purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided they are used directly in SR&ED in Canada. However, if transformed materials or trial production outputs (such as test-run fabric sold at 50% of normal price) are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC recapture (subsections 127(27)–(36)) claws back the associated credit. Lab glassware/plasticware (test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, dishes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities (unless specifically metered and documented as consumed directly in SR&ED, such as process water) are excluded as materials, though directly attributable portions may qualify as overhead under the traditional method.

For external R&D in Canada, arm's-length SR&ED contracts (for basic/applied research, experimental development, or paragraph (d) support work performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf) enter the subsection 37(1) deductible pool at 100%, but only 80% qualifies for ITC calculation. Foreign subcontracted work performed outside Canada is ineligible. Non-arm's-length (NAL) contracts do not generate ITCs directly for the payer; instead, qualified expenditures incurred by the NAL performer may be transferred using Form T1146 (Line 546), excess assistance is allocated via Form T1145 (Line 540), and NAL property/service acquisitions are adjusted under subsection 127(11.6) (Line 543). Third-party payments—direct funding, student/employee sponsorship, or payments in kind to CRA-approved universities, colleges, research institutes, associations, granting councils, or tax-exempt Canadian non-profit SR&ED corporations—also qualify at 80% for ITCs where the SR&ED is conducted in Canada, relates to the claimant's business, and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results, documented per payment on Form T1263.
3.4 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Rules

Enacted Bill C-15 restored three capital and equipment-leasing avenues for property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. First, Full SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Line 390 and Part 6B of Form T661) cover depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, where the claimant intended at acquisition either to use the asset during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in SR&ED in Canada. Land (non-depreciable), buildings, and general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) are excluded. Auditors enforce a critical distinction between new and used property: while both new and used ASA depreciable property enter Line 390 for the subsection 37(1) deduction pool, used equipment is a prescribed expenditure disallowed by regulation for ITC purposes and must be deducted on Line 532. Furthermore, even within the $6,000,000 enhanced limit, the 35% ITC earned on new capital property is 40% refundable (14% cash, 21% non-refundable).

Second, under the CRA SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026; Part 6C of Form T661), Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) captures new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test, is not GPOEF, and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) (property intended at acquisition to be used over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED commercial activities). Where the new asset is used primarily (>50% of operating time) in SR&ED in Canada, 25% of its adjusted capital cost (excluding borrowed-money costs and after subsection 127(11.6) NAL adjustments and assistance reductions) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC in the First Period (from available-for-use date to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months thereafter), and an additional 25% qualifies in the Second Period (up to 50% cumulative qualified cost across both periods). Both ASA capital property and SUE trigger ITC recapture if sold or converted ASA to commercial use.

Third, under the CRA SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8 and October 7, 2026; Lines 350/355 and Part 6A, Box 759), equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 qualify (whereas building leases remain disallowed). Under the Traditional Method, leased equipment used ≥90% (ASA) of operating time in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)) is 100% claimable as a lease cost, while equipment used <90% in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)) may be claimed to the extent directly attributable on Line 360 as overhead. Under the Proxy Method, GPOEF leases are excluded, while non-GPOEF equipment leases qualify in two statutory tiers reported across Lines 350 and 355: ≥90% ASA SR&ED use (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)) and >50% primary SR&ED use (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), under which one-half of the lease cost qualifies.

body.text: 4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credits and Assistance Interaction
4.1 Federal-Provincial Assistance "Grind" Mechanics and Strategic Renunciation

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces ("grinds") both the federal subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures in the taxation year earned. Provincial statutes, by contrast, do not treat the federal SR&ED ITC as assistance reducing provincial eligible expenditures. Because of this one-way federal grind, combined federal-provincial credit rates are multiplicative rather than additive. Moreover, if an unprofitable CCPC claims a non-refundable provincial credit (such as Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC, British Columbia's 10% non-refundable credit above $3,000,000, or Saskatchewan's 10% non-refundable tier), every $100 of unusable non-refundable provincial credit grinds federal qualified expenditures by $100, forfeiting $35 of immediate federal cash refund. To prevent cash loss, Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Nova Scotia allow claimants to formally renounce provincial R&D credits—generally on or before the federal T2 filing-due date (6 months after tax year-end)—preserving 100% of the federal expenditure base.
4.2 Québec's Modernized CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025 Taxation Years)

Announced in the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget and administered by Revenu Québec on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (with Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated-group allocation and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization details), the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) applies to taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. CRIC abolished and replaced eight legacy Québec tax measures: the R&D salaries and wages credit, the university/public research centre/consortium research credit, the consortium fees and dues credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, the technological adaptation services credit, the industrial design component of the design tax credit (while retaining fashion design), and the personal tax holidays for foreign researchers and foreign experts.

Available to corporations operating a business and maintaining an establishment in Québec (regardless of asset size), the CRIC is 100% refundable, paying 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above an annual exclusion threshold and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier. The annual exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 (prorated for short years) or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 for 2025) for each eligible employee, prorated strictly by the percentage of time each employee devoted to eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. Beyond core R&D, CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities performed in Québec in conjunction with Québec R&D: (i) regulatory testing, technological validations, and studies for initial commercialization approval or certification, and (ii) product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and material selection). Qualified Québec expenditures comprise 100% of eligible employee wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor contracts, 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, consortia, or university entities, and 100% of new depreciable capital property used almost exclusively (≥90%) in Québec R&D/pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, used equipment, and large-investment-project holiday assets; cannot be combined with Québec's C3i credit on the same expense, and advisory commentary notes rate reductions for intercompany outsourcing where related-party revenue exceeds 50%). Separately, Québec's refocused AI-oriented Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (TCEB) continues at a 30% total rate split in tax practitioner summaries as 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025, 22% / 8% in 2026, 21% / 9% in 2027, and 20% / 10% in 2028.
4.3 Ontario, Western, Atlantic, and Northern Provincial/Territorial Regimes

Administered by the CRA alongside the T2 return for corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment, Ontario maintains three distinct credits. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — T2 Schedule 566) provides CCPCs an 8% fully refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario expenditures (maximum $240,000 refund), phasing out between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (full phase-out rules appear on Schedule 566); because Ontario did not mirror Bill C-15's $6,000,000 cap, Ontario CCPC spending between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000 earns the 35% federal credit without the 8% OITC. The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — T2 Schedule 508) provides all Ontario corporations a 3.5% non-refundable credit subject to recapture and timely renunciation. Finally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — T2 Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 per associated group (maximum $4,000,000 refund) for eligible contracts with designated Ontario Eligible Research Institutes, excluding salaries of ERI staff connected to the claimant.

Across Western, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, Alberta administers its Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provincially under sections 26.95–26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, filed within 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date), delivering a 100% refundable credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D spending equal to 8% up to the corporation's prior two-year average Alberta R&D base and 20% on incremental spending above that base. Among CRA-administered regimes, British Columbia (Form T666, Income Tax Act (BC) ss. 97–103; 18-month deadline) offers a 10% refundable credit to CCPCs up to $3,000,000 (max $300,000) and a 10% non-refundable credit otherwise (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward; renounceable); Manitoba (T2 Schedule 380, Income Tax Act (MB) s. 7.3; 18-month deadline) offers a 15% credit that is half refundable (7.5%) and half non-refundable (7.5%) for in-house R&D (3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward) and 100% refundable (15%) for qualifying Manitoba institute contracts (with Manitoba educational contracts 100% eligible rather than 80%); Saskatchewan (T2 Schedule 403, Income Tax Act (SK) ss. 63–63.4) offers CCPCs a 10% refundable credit up to $1,000,000 and 10% non-refundable above $1,000,000 or for non-CCPCs (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward); Nova Scotia (T2 Schedule 340, Income Tax Act (NS) s. 41; 18-month deadline) and Newfoundland and Labrador (covering corporations, individuals, trusts, and partners) each provide uncapped 15% fully refundable credits; and Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable credit to corporations and Yukon-resident individuals plus an additional 5% (20% total) on payments to Yukon University. New Brunswick (T2 Schedule 360) offers a CRA-administered 15% fully refundable R&D corporate tax credit, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut offer no R&D tax credits.

body.text: To illustrate federal-provincial grind math in practice: in Ontario (renouncing the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC), a Qualifying CCPC incurring $500,000 of qualified current SR&ED expenditures earns $40,000 in 8% refundable OITC, leaving $460,000 for the 35% federal enhanced ITC ($161,000), for a combined cash refund of $201,000 (40.20%) rather than a naive 43% ($215,000); at $6,000,000 of qualified Ontario spending, OITC caps at $240,000 (8% × $3,000,000), leaving $5,760,000 for the 35% federal ITC ($2,016,000) and yielding $2,256,000 (37.60% blended). In Québec under CRIC, a Qualifying CCPC paying $500,000 in direct R&D salaries across two full-time R&D researchers (where the $50,000 minimum exceeds two 2025 basic personal amounts of 2 × $18,571 = $37,142) claims 30% CRIC on $450,000 = $135,000; its federal proxy-method qualified base of $775,000 ($500,000 wages + $275,000 PPA) is ground by $135,000 to $640,000, earning $224,000 (35% × $640,000) federally for a combined cash refund of $359,000 (71.80% of cash payroll).
5. Governing Authorities, Prescribed Forms, Deadlines, and Pre-Claim Approval
5.1 Institutional Governance and 2026 Prescribed Tax Form Updates

While the Department of Finance Canada formulates tax policy, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers federal (and harmonized provincial/territorial) SR&ED claims through Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) staffed by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and Financial Reviewers (FRs). Following Bill C-15's Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the CRA released updated prescribed forms and policies between May and October 2026, alongside Fall 2026 upgrades to the digital SR&ED Client Portal (inside My Business Account) and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool.

body.text: 5.2 Statutory Filing Deadlines and Absolute Forfeiture Rules

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1) and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file prescribed forms (Form T661 and T2 Schedule 31 or personal/partnership equivalents) containing all prescribed information on or before 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date. For corporations, whose T2 filing-due date is 6 months after taxation year-end, the absolute SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (though filing at the 6-month T2 due date accelerates refunds and preserves 6-month provincial credit renunciation windows). For individuals and trusts, the deadline is 12 months after their respective tax return filing-due dates (generally 17.5 months after year-end for sole proprietors according to accounting firm guidance, noting that Budget 2026 proposes shifting certain personal filing dates to May 15 starting in the 2027 tax year), while partnerships must file within 12 months after the earliest filing-due date of their members' income tax returns for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends. Missing this reporting deadline—whether on an original or amended claim—results in permanent, non-discretionary forfeiture: unfiled or late-filed outlays are deemed never to be SR&ED expenditures and earn zero ITCs.
5.3 CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Review Service Standards

Launched on April 1, 2026 pursuant to Budget 2025, the CRA's optional Pre-Claim Approval process provides binding up-front project eligibility determinations before work begins or costs are incurred. Eligibility is open to CCPCs, Canadian corporations, and Canadian partnerships in good standing with the CRA that have annual gross income under $25,000,000. Applications follow a four-step workflow:

items: Submit a brief online web request (<5 minutes) to receive a CRA case number within 2 to 5 business days.
Complete the application inside My Business Account using existing project documentation for up to three projects.
Attend a technical meeting with a CRA SR&ED specialist within four weeks of submission (mandatory for new SR&ED claimants; optional at CRA's discretion for returning claimants in good standing).
Receive an official written eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks of completing the My Business Account application.

body.text: Approved pre-claim determinations remain valid for up to three years. Furthermore, when a filed SR&ED claim containing pre-approved projects is selected for an expenditure-only review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days (unless the executed project diverged significantly from the approved scope or non-pre-approved projects were added). For standard refundable claims selected for CRA review (estimated by tax practitioners at roughly 20% of claims), the published CRA service standard is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (targeted 90% of the time), whereas accounting firm estimates place unreviewed refund processing at roughly 60 to 120 days, and non-refundable reviewed claims carry no published service standard.
6. Judicial Precedents, CRA Eligibility Guidelines, and Audit Defence Standards
6.1 Foundational Jurisprudence and Modern Federal Court of Appeal Rulings

Every CRA technical review and Tax Court of Canada appeal is governed by the five-question common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) (at para. 16):

items: Was there a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Did the overall procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulating and testing hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Did the process result in (or aim to achieve) a scientific or technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: Although the CRA archived its 2015 Eligibility of Work policy on August 16, 2021 and reframed its administrative guidelines around the simplified "Why" and "How" requirements, the Federal Court of Appeal has repeatedly held that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1). Building on foundational appellate rulings in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (December 1998, FCA) and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria articulate the statutory meaning of subsection 248(1) rather than imposing extra-statutory hurdles.

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47), a software consulting claimant proved technological uncertainty before the Tax Court yet lost because it failed the remaining Northwest Hydraulic criteria. Dismissing the appeal, Justice Rennie confirmed that: (a) CRA's August 2021 "Why and How" guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method (which courts apply flexibly in a manner suitable for applied sciences and the claimant's business environment); (b) records judged "vague," "unclear," and lacking a logical progression between experimental premise and result are fatal; and (c) expert reports opining on the ultimate legal question of SR&ED eligibility risk inadmissibility. In Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, the Tax Court again synthesized Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, CW Agencies, Kam-Press, and National R&D as the settled Canadian legal standard.

body.text: 6.2 CRA Technical and Financial Review Protocols and Contemporaneous Documentation

Under the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and Program Financial Claim Review Manual, CRA audits examine either both technical eligibility and expenditures or expenditures alone. During a Technical Review, RTAs issue transparent Requests for Information (RFIs), interview hands-on technical employees regarding specific tasks, schedules, and technological problems, and verify that all five Northwest Hydraulic questions are answered in the affirmative. Defensible contemporaneous evidence includes dated project planning and design documents, laboratory notebooks, source-code repositories, test logs linking hypotheses to outcomes, meeting minutes, and post-December 15, 2024 equipment operating-time logs substantiating ≥90% ASA capital/lease claims and >50% SUE primary use.

During a Financial Review, CRA Financial Reviewers audit general-ledger reconciliations, employee time-tracking records, proof of wage payment within 180 days of year-end, Canadian contractor agreements (verifying domestic execution and stripping pre-December 16, 2024 capital elements), specified-employee YMPE caps, assistance reductions, and future ITC recapture triggers (transformed materials and capital/SUE commercial conversions), with heightened internal review triggered where permanent income adjustments exceed ±$2,000,000 or permanent tax/audit net-present-value changes exceed ±$400,000. Unresolved review disputes may be escalated internally to CTSO Technical/Financial Managers before assessment, contested via a formal Notice of Objection to CRA Appeals, and appealed to the Tax Court of Canada.
